TI Introduction to the Special Series: Examining the Special Education
   Research Base
SO REMEDIAL AND SPECIAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE special education; research methodology; evidence-based practice
ID PUBLICATION BIAS; SCIENCE; INCENTIVES; PREVALENCE; STANDARDS; INCREASE;
   TRUTH
AB This introduction to the special series, Examining the Special Education Research Base, situates the work within broader concerns about questionable research practices and the reproducibility crisis in science. We review lessons from other fields, summarize existing meta-research in special education, and provide an overview of three reviews examining publication bias, selective outcome reporting, and the scarcity of null findings. Shared themes suggest that although the special education field appears to have fewer problems than some disciplines, potential threats to the validity of the special education research base were identified. We conclude by highlighting the implications of the three reviews for research and practice, and calling for the greater adoption of open-science practices to strengthen the evidence base in special education.

TI The instrumentalisation of physical education by the Estado Novo
   Regime in Portugal (1933-1974)
SO SPORT EDUCATION AND SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Estado novo; physical education; dictatorship; Mocidade Portuguesa;
   Portugal
AB The Estado Novo was a dictatorial, authoritarian, and autocratic regime that prevailed in Portugal for 41 uninterrupted years until the Carnation Revolution on April 25, 1974. The regime aimed to create an ideal society founded on the principles of God, Country, and Family. The goal was to form disciplined, rigorous, obedient, and simultaneously healthy bodies, so it was critical to make the formative nature of physical education mandatory at all educational levels in school. When the Estado Novo was implemented, the training of specialists in physical education was accredited by courses taught at the Lisbon Geography Society and the Army School of Physical Education. However, the military instruction seemed eager to establish itself as the main reference in the field of physical education. The Organiza & ccedil;& atilde;o Nacional Mocidade Portuguesa (a militia organisation aimed at young people) was established in 1936 in reaction to the convictions of a regime that was deeply concerned with the ideological framework and discipline of Portuguese youngster, crucial to the process of disciplining bodies. This article explores how the Estado Novo used physical education in the period 1933-1974 with the aim of ensuring that it served the regime's training purposes and perpetuated nationalist ideals.

TI Toward a theory of trauma-informed pedagogy in higher education
SO TEACHING IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Trauma; trauma-informed pedagogy; engaged pedagogy; therapeutic
   education; bell hooks
ID LIFE EVENTS; COLLEGE; BODY
AB In response to the prevalence of trauma exposure in college-going cohorts, scholars have adapted trauma-informed care's core values (safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment) to pedagogical practice in higher education. Trauma-informed pedagogy (TIP) seeks to provide opportunities for meaningful learning by minimizing disruptions to both cognitive functioning and relationships within the classroom. However, higher education scholars working within the trauma-informed paradigm have noted an absence of a consistent and coherent theoretical framework for TIP. This conceptual paper seeks to address this issue by proposing a theoretical framework for trauma-informed pedagogical scholarship moving forward. It does so by drawing out nascent theoretical commitments in the literature, engaging with global critiques of 'therapeutic' educational interventions, and situating TIP in relation to critical and holistic pedagogical theories, particularly bell hooks' theory of engaged pedagogy. I conclude by inviting others to re-examine bell hooks' work and to further theorize trauma-informed teaching and learning.

TI The big data paradox and significance
SO TEACHING STATISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE big data; effect size; independence; population; power; sample;
   significance; variation
AB More data does not necessarily mean more information: this is the big data paradox, and it should be more widely disseminated as the essential point is that caution should be exercised regarding inferences made in areas where large amounts of data are routinely used, such as data mining and artificial intelligence. In this article, the assumptions underpinning methods of statistical inference are considered, and whilst departures from these assumptions may have little effect when the amount of data (sample size) is relatively small, there can be substantial cumulative effects from increasing sample size. Consideration is also given to assessing any practical significance from the effect size relative to variation in the population to which any inferences might apply. Emphasizing assumptions and exploring their effects could (should?) be incorporated as adjunct material in lectures/classes on statistical inference.

TI Reconceptualising cleft habitus: belonging and inclusion at Australian
   regional universities
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Cleft habitus; Academics; Insider/outsider; Regional; University; Higher
   education
ID AUTOETHNOGRAPHY; WOMEN
AB An autoethnographic exploration of the life and career experiences of ten academics across the Australian Regional University Network (RUN) unearthed a prevailing disjuncture between formative cultural experiences and academia that expands upon Binns' revised notion of cleft habitus. It signifies a gap between the generative capacity of cleft experience and its predominant construction in the literature as loss, difficulty and perceived deficit. Drawing on a framework that combines 'cleft habitus' and principles of intersectionality, this paper examines how cleft experiences impact study and academic work in higher education. Key findings include how academics within a cleft habitus space occupy liminal insider/outsider positions of privilege and disadvantage and can leverage insights gained from these experiences to inform their broad scholarly practice. Reconceptualising cleft habitus as a resource provides a new contribution to discourses around equity, diversity and inclusion in higher education.

TI The Queer Failure of Diversity Coursework
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE diversity requirement; diversity coursework; queer failure; queer
   pedagogy; discomfort
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; STUDENTS; WORKING; IMPACT; COLOR
AB This article provides a theoretical argument for a queer failure pedagogy enacted in required diversity courses. Queer failure, as originally theorized by Halberstam (2011), rejects the traditional notion of success and failure rooted in capitalist, heteropatriarchal hierarchies. Queer- and critical disability-informed educators have taken this concept and theorized what this approach can open up for educators in the classroom. This article is particularly interested in understanding failure in the required diversity course, as failure is a constant presence when having discussions on diversity, equity, and inclusion in today's political climate. This article offers examples of the author's experience engaging with queer failure and discomfort and explores how we can reframe this crisis for ourselves and our students.

TI Supporting women in relation to menopause knowledge and awareness:
   Lessons learned from a gender-specific educational programme
SO HEALTH EDUCATION JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Evaluation; health education; menopause; women; voluntary and community
   sector
ID SYMPTOMS
AB Background: International evidence suggests that women experience a range of health and wellbeing challenges during menopause, and perimenopause. Current literature highlights the need for women to be educated about menopause, yet limited evidence exists in England about community-based menopause programmes that focus on educating women on this issue.Study's objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate a gender-specific (women-only) menopause-focused educational programme delivered in one English local authority area.Setting: A bespoke educational programme on menopause was delivered to women (n = 146) living in one geographical area, via 10 voluntary and community sector organisations, between July 2023 and March 2024.Method: This mixed methods, co-produced evaluation gathered data using pre- and post-course questionnaires (n = 51), learning logs (n = 7), observations of meetings (n = 5) and semi-structured interviews (professionals n = 11; course attendees, n = 7). Differences between pre- and post-test scores were calculated using the Wilcoxon signed rank test and effect sizes were identified. Qualitative data were analysed thematically.Results: The programme met its aims. The evaluation data show that this community-based, women-only educational programme was valued by delivery partners and course attendees alike, all of whom noted learning through their participation. Women as course attendees increased their knowledge and were able to use this education to improve their health.Conclusion: The programme worked well for the women who accessed it. However, it did not reach all the women who may have needed it, and it was only funded for a short while. Longer term, more sustainable educational provision to educate and inform women about menopause is required.

TI Towards a process-oriented assessment of computational thinking:
   behavioural data and machine learning approach
SO INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
LA English
DT Article
DE CT assessment; behavioural data; clustering; Bebras interactive tasks;
   machine learning
AB Computational thinking (CT) is increasingly recognised as a vital skill for the twenty-first century. However, the lack of reliable assessment tools continues to create significant challenges for assessing students' CT skills effectively. This study uses behavioural data from the interactive Bebras Challenge task to assess CT skills, offering a deep analysis of the problem-solving process beyond final binary outcomes. The dataset of solutions (N = 336) from an interactive CT task, focusing on recorded behavioural data, such as object interactions, decision sequences, colour choices and time taken to complete the task, was analysed. Machine learning algorithms were applied to cluster the solutions, identifying distinct patterns that reflected different problem-solving strategies. The analysis went beyond binary classification, revealing variations in solution approaches within successful and unsuccessful attempts, allowing for a more detailed assessment of CT skills. The findings from this study suggest a scoring system based on identified solution clusters as a more refined assessment of CT compared to existing binary methods. This underscores the potential of behavioural data to improve CT assessment.

TI Effects of a VR-based blended approach on tourist geographic literacy,
   satisfaction, and problem-solving in geography field trips
SO INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; geography field trips; experiential learning cycle;
   inquiry-based learning; problem-solving process
ID EXPERIENCES; ENVIRONMENTS; INQUIRY; MODEL; TOOL
AB Geography field trips offer students opportunities to step outside the classroom, fostering the development of their observational and problem-solving skills. However, without adequent preparation and clear objectives, students' engagement, experience, and learning effectiveness during the field trip are often compromised. Therefore, this study integrated inquiry-based learning and Kolb's experiential learning cycle to propose a virtual reality-based blended approach for geography field trips (VR-BF). Thirty middle school students were recruited to participate in a quasi-experiment and were randomly assigned to either an experimental group (EG) that underwent the VR-BF approach or a control group (CG) that was exposed to the video-based blended approach for geography field trips. The results indicated that the EG in the VR-BF intervention demonstrated significantly higher posttest scores than the CG in travel geospatial recognition and tourist satisfaction. Moreover, it was also found that students in the EG integrated external resources better than those in the CG during problem solving. The epistemic network analysis (ENA) showed that students in the EG demonstrated a higher cognitive level. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of the VR-BF approach and provides pedagogical insights and practical references for future research on geography field trips.

TI Comparing Peer Feedback and Generative Artificial Intelligence Feedback
   in Japanese English as a Foreign Language Speaking Context: Impacts on
   Motivation, Engagement, and Writing Self-Efficacy
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE engagement; feedback; GenAI; motivation; self-efficacy
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; STUDENTS; SYSTEM
AB This study explores the comparative effectiveness of peer feedback and generative AI (GenAI) feedback on Japanese university students learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL), specifically examining their motivation, engagement, and writing self-efficacy during script-writing preparation for speaking tasks. Acknowledging the close relationship between speaking and writing, as well as the essential role of feedback in second language acquisition (SLA), the research contrasts the impact of peer feedback during the first semester with GenAI feedback, particularly through ChatGPT, in the second semester. The primary objective was to assess whether students experienced increased motivation, enhanced writing self-efficacy, and greater engagement after transitioning to GenAI feedback, while also investigating their perceptions of using ChatGPT. A survey was conducted with 147 first- and second-year university students at three intervals throughout the academic year to evaluate these factors. Results revealed a statistically significant rise in students' ideal L2 self following the introduction of GenAI feedback. Writing self-efficacy improved significantly after peer feedback and remained high after the shift to GenAI feedback. Additionally, students reported notably higher affective and behavioral engagement with GenAI feedback compared to peer feedback, although cognitive engagement did not show significant differences. Qualitative responses highlighted benefits such as immediate error detection and improvement suggestions, alongside concerns regarding over-reliance and the absence of human interaction. The findings indicate that GenAI feedback can effectively enhance motivation and both affective and behavioral engagement in EFL speaking preparation, serving as a complementary tool to traditional feedback methods. This study underscores the pedagogical implications of thoughtfully integrating GenAI tools into EFL instruction, emphasizing the importance of careful prompt design and instructor support while recognizing the limitations of the current study's design.

   Regulatory Focus and Teacher Feedback
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF APPLIED LINGUISTICS
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 writing; regulatory fit; regulatory focus; teacher feedback; writing
   motivation; (sic)(sic) (sic)(sic)(sic); (sic)(sic) (sic)(sic);
   (sic)(sic)(sic) (sic)(sic); (sic)(sic) (sic)(sic)(sic); L2
   (sic)(sic)(sic)
ID WRITTEN CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK; LEARNER ENGAGEMENT; STUDENT ENGAGEMENT;
   PERFORMANCE; DECISION
AB Focusing on the learner's agency in feedback practices, this study investigates how learners' regulatory focus (i.e., promotion- vs. prevention-oriented) and teacher feedback interact to affect second language (L2) writing motivation. It examines the effects of regulatory fit on L2 learners' writing motivation and self-evaluation of writing performance. TI Making Peace with Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Art Education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; art education; artificial intelligence; dialogue;
   ecologies; peace
AB Views regarding the access, position and use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and AI pedagogies in transformative art education are changeable and controversial, particularly regarding influence, opportunity and ethics. This dialogic paper grapples with these concerns to 'make peace' with AI and its pedagogic development in art education. It draws on collective intelligence and collective imagination gained from scholarly material, the machine and art educator reflective experiences and voices to position 'peaceful dialogic making' as a pedagogic approach to transform future art education opportunities. Making can encourage sensitive engagement with ecologies, complexities and possibilities in art education, and as demonstrated in this paper, AI can be engaged critically and with peace to enrich making. Enacting 'peaceful dialogic making' in, with, through and about AI in art education can forge identity and value connection, such as with the National Society for Education Art and Design manifesto values, that favour inclusive, equitable and lifelong art education experiences. Making peace with AI, through dialogues, roaming with it and engaging with its complexities builds responsible AI literacy that can help AI be integrated into art education aligned to contemporary and future life.

TI Assessing preschool computational thinking: relations between researcher
   instruments and educators' perspectives of learning and engagement
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EARLY YEARS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational thinking; preschool; assessment
ID ROBOTICS; TEACHER; SKILLS
AB Considerable research and policy now emphasise classroom experiences to foster computational thinking (CT) in early childhood. Despite increased interest, CT's nature and effective measurement are not fully understood. Further, research often utilises measures proctored by researchers rather than teachers. The current study, a subcomponent of a larger research-practice partnership focused on a preschool robotics programme, examines the relationship between (1) a traditional researcher-administered assessment, and (2) naturalistic teacher-administered assessments during a small group activity, both measuring CT. The study seeks to answer: What is the nature of children's performance on these measures and what are the relations between these assessments? This study includes a sample of preschoolers (n = 122 in the fall) across 7 classrooms in a large urban district who were assessed in fall and spring by members of the research team. Teachers assessed children's engagement and mastery in fall. Children demonstrated wide variability in CT. Results indicated significant growth in CT from fall to spring (t(48) = -5.56, p < .01)). Teachers' ratings of engagement were significantly correlated to children's fall CT (rho = .29, p = .02) while ratings of mastery were significantly correlated to spring CT (rho = . 32, p = .02). Implications are discussed.

TI Part of the Plan? A Critical Quantitative Examination of Mentoring and

SO JOURNAL OF DIVERSITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE graduate school; equity; computing; science, technology, engineering,

ID UNDERREPRESENTED STUDENTS; LEAKY PIPELINE; STEM; UNDERGRADUATE; SCIENCE;
   EDUCATION; IMPACT; WOMEN; COLOR; ASPIRATIONS
AB Despite decades of attention, racial/ethnic and gender inequities persist across science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medicine disciplines. In computing higher education, the disciplinary focus of this study, institutional actors must look to critical junctures between educational levels (e.g., between undergraduate and graduate degrees) to explore possible ways to disrupt processes of social reproduction. Using longitudinal data from computing undergraduate students across 15 U.S. research universities, we apply a critical quantitative lens to examine the relationship between graduate school aspirations and application behaviors. We use multiple-group structural equation modeling to focus on mediators of mentoring support and students' self-confidence for graduate school admission. Findings show that graduate education pathways vary significantly by intersecting gender and racial/ethnic identity groups, highlighting the need for equitable support in computing departments (especially among Women of Color). We offer implications for both institutional practitioners and larger policy intermediaries, as well as a discussion of theoretical and empirical needs to continue resolving disparities in computing fields and disrupt the mechanisms that turn highly qualified computing students away from graduate education.

TI "It Feels Isolating": Exploring the Experiences of Work Among Counselors
   of Color at Predominantly White Institutions in the United States
SO JOURNAL OF DIVERSITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE counselors of color; predominantly White institutions; university
   counseling center; professional burnout; workplace experiences
ID CRITICAL RACE THEORY; MICROAGGRESSIONS; EDUCATION
AB Although scholarly attention to the experiences of mental health professionals of color has grown, limited research has focused specifically on those serving as mental health counselors within university counseling centers at predominantly White institutions in the United States. These counselors navigate institutional settings shaped by structural inequities and racialized dynamics that create significant professional barriers. Examining their experiences is crucial for understanding the factors that contribute to burnout, turnover, and the delivery of culturally responsive mental health services to increasingly diverse student populations. This study addressed this gap by exploring the lived experiences of eight counselors of color working in university counseling centers at predominantly White institutions, using interpretative phenomenological analysis of semistructured interviews. We identified three master themes: Pushbackagainst diversity, equity, and inclusion in higher education, unrecognized burden of counselors of color, and unrecognized burden of counselors of color. Findings highlight the systemic challenges these counselors face, including institutional resistance to diversity, equity, and inclusion, hostility and discrimination in the workplace, and the implicit burden of diversity work, while also underscoring the importance of support systems as a way of resistance and coping. Implications for fostering equitable, inclusive, and sustainable counseling environments are discussed.

TI Teacher Coaching in Upper Secondary School: Examining the Effects on
   Teacher-Student Interaction and Student Engagement
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE complier average causal effect; intent to treat; INTERACT intervention;
   teacher coaching; teacher-student interaction
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; PARTNER-SECONDARY; ACHIEVEMENT;
   IMPLEMENTATION; INTERVENTION; INSTRUCTION; OUTCOMES; METAANALYSIS;
   PSYCHOLOGY; EDUCATION
AB In a cluster randomized control trial, we investigated the effects of video-based teacher coaching (INTERACT) on the quality of teacher-student interactions (TSIs) and student engagement among upper secondary school students (n = 1,341). Ninety-eight teachers from 12 schools were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 49) or the practice-as-usual group. Teachers in the intervention group were assigned to a coach (10 coaches in total) and participated in seven coaching cycles throughout the 2022-2023 school year. Multilevel intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis indicated that the intervention had small effects, with statistically significant improvements in the three TSI domains: emotional support, classroom organization, and instructional support. However, the results indicated no significant effect or discernible impact on student emotional, behavioral, or cognitive engagement. Multilevel complier average causal effect (CACE) estimation using a combined dosage and fidelity compliance marker increased the effect sizes for the TSI domains to medium to large, and small to medium effects were documented for emotional and behavioral engagement according to Cohen's standards. For this type of intervention, these effects are considered large. For observed student engagement, the ITT analysis indicated a small intervention effect, and the CACE analysis indicated a medium effect; however, none of these effects were statistically significant. Using ITT and CACE analyses, we document both the effects of offering teacher coaching versus practice-as-usual independent of the quality of implementation, and the effects for classrooms in which the teacher implemented the intervention with high quality. Practical implications for policy and practice, as well as implications for future research, are discussed.

TI Qualitative analysis of students' perceptions of active learning
   practices in a highly structured microbiology course provides support
   for implementation of flipped and interactive classroom activities
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate; microbiology; active learning; flipped classroom;
   interactive; perceptions
ID UNDERGRADUATE SCIENCE; INTRODUCTORY PHYSICS; TEACHING-METHODS;
   ENGAGEMENT; PERFORMANCE; MODEL; MATHEMATICS; TECHNOLOGY; STRATEGIES;
   BELIEFS
AB Despite evidence that active learning practices (ALPs) increase student success and reduce the opportunity gap in historically marginalized students, lecturing alone is still being used as a primary teaching strategy. Perceptions that students do not view ALPs positively, resulting in negative course evaluations, are one of the barriers to ALP incorporation. It is unclear how students, in a highly structured course that includes diverse ALPs, perceive these practices in addition to in-person, synchronous lecturing. To fill this gap, we surveyed students in a mid-level undergraduate General Microbiology course, comprising 60-150 students, that incorporates moderate to high levels of ALPs, including interactive lecturing, collaborative work, and flipped sessions, in addition to traditional lecturing. We used inductive qualitative analysis of three open-ended questions to evaluate students' perceptions of classroom activities in terms of perceived pedagogical value (i.e., helping reach learning objectives), perceived enjoyment, and overall value of the activity (i.e., would like to see this type of activity in future courses). We show that most students perceive lecturing, followed by flipped activities, as the strategies that best help reach the learning objectives. Similarly, most students enjoy flipped activities the most and would like to see these types of activities in future courses. Students also perceive ALPs as complementary to lecture, particularly by helping improve understanding and providing opportunities to apply concepts. Our data should encourage faculty to incorporate more ALPs into their curriculum; in particular, flipped and interactive activities.

TI The impact of handwriting and typing on the reading acquisition process:
   a study using an unfamiliar orthography
SO READING AND WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Handwriting; Typing; Reading acquisition; Literacy development
ID EARLY WRITING SKILLS; WORKING-MEMORY; PHONOLOGICAL AWARENESS; LETTER
   RECOGNITION; LETTER NAMES; WORD; PREDICTORS; KNOWLEDGE; PRESCHOOL;
   LITERACY
AB Although there is evidence of a negative impact of typing on letter learning in prereaders, it remains unclear how writing letters and words-either by hand or typing-affects reading acquisition. One possibility is that typing attenuates the recruitment of phonological recoding processes inherent in writing. To address this question, 50 kindergarten children (M age = 5.4 years) were randomly assigned to two groups: one group learned a set of novel letters and words by copying them by hand while listening to their pronunciations, whereas the other group learned the same letters and words by typing them on a computer. Both groups were assessed on three abilities reflecting different stages of reading acquisition: (a) naming the learned letters, (b) decoding novel words composed of the trained letters, and (c) visually identifying the novel words. Children in the handwriting group showed better performance in the letter naming, word decoding, and visual word identification tasks, and only in this group were phonological skills associated with learning outcomes. Regression analysis revealed that word decoding accuracy predicted word identification in the handwriting group, but this relationship was absent in the typing group. These findings suggest that writing letters and words by hand supports the development of phonological recoding skills, which are critical for forming accurate representations of words in memory.

TI Racialized Change or Nominal Absorption? Racial Equity Discourses in
   District-wide Professional Development
SO URBAN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE equity; racial discourses; racialized change work; racialized
   organizations; professional development
ID INTERMEDIARY ORGANIZATIONS; TEACHER-EDUCATION; ACCOUNTABILITY; REFORM;
   DIVERSITY; IDEOLOGY; POLITICS; CONTEXT; IMPACT; POLICY
AB This case study examines how racial equity was constructed within a district-wide professional development program. Drawing on two years of observations, interviews, and artifacts of the Equity Mentoring and Coaching (EMC) Program, it examines (a) the available equity discourses, (b) their inter- and intra-organizational influences, and (c) their incorporation. TI Teacher Digital Competence in New Zealand Primary Schools: A Qualitative
   Study of Integration Practices, Challenges, and Cultural Considerations
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher digital competence; Technology integration; Primary education;
   New Zealand; Educational equity; Culturally responsive
ID METAANALYSIS; TECHNOLOGY; IMPACT
AB This qualitative study examines the state of Teacher Digital Competence (TDC) in New Zealand primary schools through interviews with five teachers. Applying Starkey's model of digital integration and the DigCompEdu framework (Redecker in European framework for the digital competence of educators: DigCompEdu. Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg, 2017), the research reveals a spectrum of technology adoption from basic tool use to advanced pedagogical infusion. Key findings highlight technology's role in enhancing student engagement and inclusive education, while identifying persistent barriers including infrastructure limitations, professional development gaps, and equity concerns. The study particularly emphasises the underdeveloped potential of culturally responsive digital pedagogies in New Zealand's bicultural context. Findings suggest that while foundational digital competence is widespread among teachers, transformative integration remains constrained by systemic factors. The research contributes to international discussions on digital education by offering a contextualised understanding of TDC development in New Zealand's unique educational landscape, proposing recommendations for policy and practice that balance technological innovation with equity and cultural responsiveness.
